cells.tense: The picture is already built in you, and you're moving by its light.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've pictured but haven't said out loud, and say it to one person this week.
cells.core:
The picture you're working from is built out of life already lived, and that's why it holds. Plenty of people have a vision; this one has been through some rough seasons and come out shaped like something you can actually walk by. Enough light to take the next step, not much more — and that's what you're using.
What's around you is a false structure coming down fast. Not a disaster. Something that couldn't hold giving way, and the ground under it already solid enough to stand on. You may be watching what falls instead of watching the space it leaves. The next thing this is free to feed is one push in a direction you've already pictured — small, with a finish line, made today.
cells.sheetLine: You dream from experience, and the ground is already open.
cells.verb: moving through what isn't clear without forcing it clear
cells.place: where a false structure goes down fast and what's left is open

cells.tense: You're living in a version of this that hasn't arrived while the real work waits.
cells.ask: Give one thing you're tending an edge instead of more attention: cut it down to what fits a single day.
cells.core:
You've got a picture of how this ends, and you're already there, adjusting your steps to a shape that isn't here yet. The sight is real. The trouble is you've traded the room you're standing in for the one in your head, and the one in your head keeps getting more detailed the longer you stay.
What's coming down around you gets read as proof of the picture instead of just what's happening. That's where one fixed outcome starts wearing the name of what's true. The way back is care with an edge on it — tending one growing thing without clutching it, deciding what it gets and what it doesn't, and stopping there. Less holding, more room.
cells.sheetLine: You're living in the ending, and it isn't here yet.

cells.tense: You stopped reading into things, and you stand by that door even now.
cells.ask: Make one small guess about what something means, keep it to yourself, and don't check whether it's right.
cells.core:
You can still see in the dark when you let yourself, but you've quit trusting it. If it can't be measured, you don't bother, so the world arrives as plain surfaces with nothing under them. That caution is doing something for you — it's also why what's in front of you reads as blank walls.
You don't need to force a deeper read. You don't have to trust the guess, just let yourself have one. Knowing what deserves your attention comes before you can explain why, and it lands without argument if you stop arguing with it first. One small guess, kept private, is enough to start.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped reading into things, and that's why nothing moves.

cells.tense: You're already shaping how this goes, and you'd say it's just the way things went.
cells.ask: Write one sentence of what you want next and put it where you'll see it tomorrow, without telling anyone you've done it.
cells.core:
Somewhere in you there's a picture, and it's already shaping your days. Watch what you keep returning to when nobody's asking you to, and you'll catch it. But when you talk about how you got here, the story is that it happened — luck, timing, the door that was open. You're not confused about the picture. You just speak about it like it's the same as what's in the room.
It isn't. The fix is smaller than insight: one plain practice, done alone, where the picture gets its first written form. A single sentence kept where you'll find it changes what that picture is. That's the whole move.
cells.sheetLine: You're already shaping this. The shaping has no name yet.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that anything is dissolving or collapsed in the person's life — the record's seat says structures built on false premises fall when truth arrives, and none of that grants me knowledge of any collapse happening to this person. A reader could reasonably say nothing in their life is coming apart at all, and the readings must survive that. The acts stay doable if I'm wrong about them: each one is a camera-visible thing done today, costing nothing, needing no one safe on hand — except the third, which asks them to try a small guess in private, and stays useful even if the guess is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them is the one that would sell the seat as a thing happening to them rather than a place they're standing; I've cut it. My ongoing risk is saying what happened back there, who, or how long ago — the cells locate, they never narrate.
